clue.text: Artists tucked into basic mashed vegetable

indicators.note: something tucked into another thing sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other
mashed food is pulped out of its original shape, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: taken as written
RA is a Royal Academician, so artists are RAs

explanation.surface: Painters sitting down to a plain plate of mashed veg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Artists' looks like the diners in the scene, but it is the crossword staple for Royal Academicians, and 'basic' is only letters to mash.
explanation.definitionFit: Brassica is the botanical genus of cabbages, broccoli and sprouts, all common vegetables.

clue.text: Old college's talking parrot

indicators.note: talking means we go by how the next word is spoken, not spelt

parts.note: Polly is the stock name for a pet parrot

explanation.surface: An old college keeps a parrot that can talk.
explanation.walkthrough: A poly was a British polytechnic, a higher-education college upgraded to university status in 1992; 'Polly wants a cracker' is the classic parrot line.
explanation.definitionFit: Poly is the short form of polytechnic, a type of British college that no longer exists under that name.

clue.text: Scrap over editors' accommodation

indicators.note: one thing placed over another covers it on both sides, so it wraps around the next piece

parts.note: a scrap is a small bit
ED is the standard abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: An argument over where the newspaper editors should be housed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrap' looks like a fight or a verb to cancel, but it is just a small piece. A bedsit is a British one-room flat used for both sleeping and living.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedsit is a single rented room serving as bedroom and sitting room, a modest form of lodging.

clue.text: Star wearing cap at centre of Mexican wave

indicators.note: a person wearing a hat is covered by it, so the headgear goes around the star

parts.note: a tam is a Scottish woollen cap
the Sun is our nearest star

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the fourth of seven letters sits in the middle

explanation.surface: A celebrity in a cap joins a Mexican wave in the middle of a stadium crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mexican wave' reads as the crowd ritual, but 'wave' alone is the definition and 'Mexican' just supplies its middle letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A tsunami is a huge sea wave set off by an earthquake or undersea landslide.

clue.text: Capital where servant gets to grips with Latin way to express gratitude

indicators.note: to get to grips with something is to grasp it, holding it inside one's hands

parts.note: a valet is a manservant
L is the standard abbreviation for Latin
ta is informal British for thanks

explanation.surface: A city where a servant struggles to learn how to say thank you in Latin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Latin way to express gratitude' reads as one phrase, but Latin gives only L and the thanks is the British 'ta'.
explanation.definitionFit: Valletta is the capital city of Malta, on the island's northeast coast.

clue.text: Maroon fuel spilt in racing championship

indicators.note: spilt liquid splashes all over, so the letters end up scattered in a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A maroon-coloured car leaks petrol during a motor race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maroon' looks like a colour or a verb to strand, but it is only letters for the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Formula One is the top world motor-racing series, contested as an annual drivers' and constructors' championship.

clue.text: Setter close to vintner given consignment of wine

parts.note: the setter refers to themself as me

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is kept

parts.note: its final letter
a lot is a batch of goods for sale

explanation.surface: The crossword setter sits near a wine merchant who has received a shipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' is the crossword compiler, giving ME as in many clues.
explanation.definitionFit: Merlot is a red grape variety and the red wine made from it.

clue.text: Nun providing media coverage of 2016 Olympic venue

indicators.note: coverage wraps around something, so the media word goes around the venue

parts.note: the press is the news media
Rio de Janeiro hosted the 2016 Summer Olympics

explanation.surface: A nun turns out to be a journalist reporting on the Rio Olympics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coverage' sounds like reporting, but it marks one piece wrapping another.
explanation.definitionFit: A prioress is a nun in charge of a priory, a female religious superior.

clue.text: Destroy cave to get bird

indicators.note: something destroyed is wrecked and could be rebuilt in another form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone wrecks a cave in order to catch a bird roosting there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get' reads as purpose, but 'to' is part of the letters being rearranged and only 'get' links.
explanation.definitionFit: The avocet is a black-and-white wading bird with a long upcurved bill, emblem of the RSPB.

clue.text: Look inside ladies' pyjamas!

indicators.note: inside says the letters sit within the following words, spanning them

parts.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A cheeky invitation to peek inside women's nightwear.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark plays up the naughty surface; the answer runs across ladiES PYjamas.
explanation.definitionFit: To espy is to catch sight of something, so it is a literary verb for looking or spotting.

clue.text: Man gets ill after demolishing whisky

indicators.note: after demolition a building is in pieces and could be put back together differently

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A man feels sick after knocking back a bottle of whisky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Demolishing' suggests drinking a whole bottle, but it tells us to break up the opening three words.
explanation.definitionFit: Single malt is Scotch whisky made from malted barley at one distillery, so it is a type of whisky.

clue.text: Gastropod with soft elegant shell

parts.note: limp means floppy or not firm

indicators.note: a shell is the outside of something, so only the outer letters of the word are kept

parts.note: its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A snail-like creature with a delicate, graceful shell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shell' fits the sea creature perfectly, but here it strips a word to its outside letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The limpet is a marine gastropod mollusc with a conical shell that clings to rocks.

clue.text: Fragile pot damaged with rake

indicators.note: a damaged pot is broken, and its pieces can be reassembled in another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A delicate flowerpot gets broken by a garden rake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rake' reads as a garden tool but means a dissolute man about town.
explanation.definitionFit: A rake is a reckless, immoral pleasure-seeker, and a profligate is a wildly extravagant, dissolute person.

clue.text: Butcher's ultimate ruin?

indicators.note: a ruin is a wrecked version of something, so the letters are knocked out of order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A question about what finally ruins a butcher's trade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butcher's' looks like a possessive noun; it is the verb 'butcher' followed by 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: To butcher someone is to hack or cut them savagely, which is what mutilating does.

clue.text: Old man with attitude protecting Mexico's last native American youngster

parts.note: one's old man is one's father, pa

indicators.note: protecting something means surrounding and shielding it, so one piece goes around the other

parts.note: a pose is an attitude struck

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, the only one kept

parts.note: its final letter

explanation.surface: An old father with a protective attitude shields a young child.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old man' is British slang for father. The answer word is now considered dated.
explanation.definitionFit: A papoose is a baby or young child of a North American Indigenous people, especially one carried on the back.

clue.text: Guards found in small passageways between houses

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small
in northern English, an entry is a narrow alley between terraced houses

explanation.surface: Security guards lurking in the narrow alleys between houses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'found in' reads like a container signal, but it only links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Sentries are soldiers posted to keep watch, so they are guards on duty.

clue.text: Leave Virginia with American deer

parts.note: VA is the postal abbreviation for Virginia
moose is the North American name for the largest deer

explanation.surface: Someone departs the state of Virginia accompanied by a moose.
explanation.definitionFit: Vamoose is slang for clear off or depart hurriedly, from Spanish vamos, so it means to leave.

clue.text: Topping of signature dish making a splash

indicators.note: the topping of a down entry's word is its top, so only its first letter is kept

parts.note: its first letter
a platter is a large serving dish

explanation.surface: A chef's signature dish with a topping that makes a big impression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topping' sounds like a garnish and 'making a splash' like a hit, but the topping is one letter and splash is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A splatter is a messy spray of liquid, so as a noun it is a splash.

clue.text: Grape trained around sides of oval framework for plants

indicators.note: around says one piece is wrapped about the other
a trained vine is bent into a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the sides of a word are its two ends, so only first and last letters are kept

parts.note: its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A grapevine trained around an oval garden frame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trained' is the gardener's word for guiding a vine, and here also signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: A pergola is an arched garden structure of posts and beams over which climbing plants are grown.

clue.text: Tongue of Henry VIII's wife cut by weapon

indicators.note: a cut name is trimmed short, so its last letter is lopped off

parts.note: Catherine Parr was Henry VIII's sixth and last wife
a lance is a long cavalry spear

explanation.surface: Henry VIII's queen has her tongue cut by a weapon, a grisly Tudor scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut by weapon' looks like an insertion, but 'cut' only trims PARR and 'by' places the weapon beside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tongue can mean a language or way of speaking, and parlance is a particular manner of speech or jargon.

clue.text: American drug smuggler going to Thailand for protection from harm

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for American
a mule is someone who carries illegal drugs across a border
T is the international vehicle code for Thailand

explanation.surface: An American drug courier flies to Thailand hoping not to get caught.
explanation.definitionFit: An amulet is a charm or trinket worn as a safeguard against evil, danger or disease.

clue.text: Nasty slime covering universal breakfast dish

indicators.note: covering something means wrapping around it, so one piece encloses the other
something nasty is foul and messed up, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
U is the film classification for universal viewing

explanation.surface: A disgusting slime spread over a bowl of cereal everyone eats.
explanation.walkthrough: U as universal comes from the British film-rating system, where U films suit all ages.
explanation.definitionFit: Muesli is a Swiss mix of oats, nuts and dried fruit eaten with milk in the morning.

clue.text: Roman's capsized sailor's vessel

indicators.note: a capsized boat is turned upside down, so in a down entry the word is read bottom to top

parts.note: a Rom is a Romany man, a gypsy
tar is old slang for a sailor

explanation.surface: A Roman's boat has overturned, and a sailor owns it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roman' looks like someone from Rome, but read as Romany it gives the gypsy word Rom. 'Vessel' suggests a ship but means a bowl.
explanation.definitionFit: A mortar is a sturdy bowl in which substances are ground with a pestle, so it is a kitchen vessel.

clue.text: Move to European capital and run into bird

parts.note: to budge is to move slightly
Riga is the capital of Latvia
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Someone relocates to a European capital and runs into a bird there.
explanation.walkthrough: 'run into' reads as meeting by chance, but 'run' is one letter and 'into' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The budgerigar is a small Australian parakeet, widely kept as a pet bird.

clue.text: Fruit stone with hard white inner layer

parts.note: the pit is the stone of a fruit like a cherry
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A fruit stone sits within a hard white inner layer.
explanation.walkthrough: The fruity surface makes 'white inner layer' sound part of the description; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Pith is the spongy white tissue lining the rind of citrus fruits beneath the coloured peel.

clue.text: Quick look up and down

parts.note: in a down light, a word that reads the same going up as going down

explanation.surface: A brief glance upwards and downwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up and down' sounds like scanning someone, but it says the answer reads the same either way in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A peep is a brief furtive glance, a fleeting look at something.

clue.text: Pressure warped steel in 22's partner

parts.note: P is the physics symbol for pressure

indicators.note: warped metal is bent out of shape, so its letters are twisted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Pressure has bent the steel in a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 is MORTAR at 22 down: mortar and pestle are the classic grinding pair.
explanation.definitionFit: A pestle is the club-shaped tool used with a mortar, so it is the mortar's companion.

clue.text: Raised fluid even breaking metal

indicators.note: breaking into something means splitting it apart and sitting inside it

parts.note: lead is a heavy metal

indicators.note: fluid things have no fixed shape, so the letters flow into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Molten metal breaking up evenly as it is lifted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fluid' fits the molten-metal picture but signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Leavened bread has been made to rise with yeast or another raising agent, so it is raised.
